questions.q: What is habitat destruction primarily caused by?
a: Human activities such as deforestation, urban expansion, agriculture, and mining
Natural volcanic eruptions exclusively
The natural migration of herbivorous animals
Normal seasonal weather changes

questions.q: What is deforestation defined as?
a: The rapid planting of new trees in urban parks
The clearing of large areas of trees without adequate replanting, leading to habitat loss and soil erosion
The natural falling of leaves in autumn
The artificial watering of greenhouse crops

questions.q: What are the major environmental consequences of large-scale deforestation?
a: Increased oxygen production and cooling of the planet
Lower carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere
Loss of biodiversity, disruption of the water cycle, soil erosion, and increased atmospheric carbon dioxide
Enhanced soil fertility and permanent forest growth

questions.q: What is pollution defined as in environmental biology?
a: The natural recycling of nutrients by bacteria
The planting of non-native vegetation
The sustainable harvesting of fish stocks
The addition of substances to the environment (air, water, or land) that cause harm or discomfort to humans and other organisms

questions.q: What causes acid rain?
a: Emissions of sulfur dioxide from burning fossil fuels and nitrogen oxides from vehicle engines dissolving in rainwater to form sulfuric and nitric acids
Excess carbon dioxide reacting with ocean water
The accumulation of plastic waste in landfills
Untreated sewage dumped into rivers

questions.q: What are the harmful ecological effects of acid rain?
a: It increases soil fertility for crops
It lowers the pH of lakes and soils, killing aquatic life, damaging tree leaves, and leaching essential mineral ions
It cures bacterial infections in fish
It causes global warming through ozone depletion

questions.q: What is eutrophication?
a: The cooling of aquatic ecosystems by industrial water
The natural cleaning of polluted lakes by bacteria

An increase in nutrient levels (nitrates and phosphates from fertilizers or sewage) in water bodies, leading to algal blooms, death of plants due to light blockage, and subsequent decomposition by bacteria that consume dissolved oxygen, suffocating aquatic animals
The accumulation of heavy metals in food chains

questions.q: What is non-biodegradable plastic pollution in oceans primarily responsible for?
a: Providing extra habitats for marine fish
Increasing water oxygen levels
Purifying toxic industrial waste
Entangling marine animals, ingestion by wildlife leading to starvation, and breakdown into microplastics that enter food chains

questions.q: What is enhanced global warming caused by?
a: An increase in greenhouse gases (such as carbon dioxide and methane) trapping outgoing thermal radiation from Earth's surface
The thinning of the ozone layer by CFCs
Excess heat generated by nuclear power plants
Normal solar flare activity

questions.q: Which of the following are the two primary greenhouse gases contributing to enhanced global warming?
a: Oxygen and nitrogen
Carbon dioxide and methane
Sulfur dioxide and helium
Hydrogen and water vapor

questions.q: What are the predicted consequences of climate change and global warming?
a: Cooling of polar ice caps and lower sea levels
Decreased extreme weather events worldwide
Melting of polar ice, rising sea levels, flooding of coastal areas, and disruption of agricultural crop yields
Permanent drought-free conditions globally

questions.q: What is bioaccumulation (or biomagnification) of toxic substances like pesticides (e.g., DDT) or heavy metals?
a: The breakdown of plastic waste by sunlight
The natural absorption of minerals by plant roots
The dilution of pollutants in large ocean currents
The progressive buildup and concentration of toxic substances in the bodies of organisms at higher trophic levels along a food chain

questions.q: What is sustainable development defined as?
a: Meeting the needs of the current generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Using all available natural resources as quickly as possible
Banning all industrial activity worldwide
Relying exclusively on non-renewable fossil fuels

questions.q: How can forests be managed sustainably?
a: Clearing entire ecosystems permanently for timber
Practicing selective logging and replanting trees (reforestation) to maintain timber supply and habitat integrity
Banning all human entry into wooded areas
Replacing trees with concrete parking lots

questions.q: What is the purpose of fish conservation and sustainable fishing practices?
a: To eliminate all commercial fishing globally
To catch as many fish as possible in a single season
To prevent overfishing by setting quotas, regulating net mesh sizes, and establishing fish breeding protected zones to ensure fish stocks replenish
To introduce invasive predator species into oceans

questions.q: Why is the conservation of endangered species important for ecosystems?
a: It prevents any natural selection from occurring
It guarantees that no animals will ever die
It increases global temperatures
To maintain biodiversity, protect complex food web stability, and preserve genetic resources for future medical and agricultural use

questions.q: What is an endangered species?
a: A species at risk of extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range
A species whose population is growing uncontrollably
A newly discovered bacterial strain
An organism that has already gone extinct

questions.q: What is the role of captive breeding programs in zoos and conservation parks?
a: To display wild animals for public entertainment exclusively
To breed endangered species in protected environments and potentially reintroduce them back into their natural habitats
To crossbreed different animal families into hybrid pets
To test new cosmetics safely

questions.q: What is an invasive species?
a: A native species that migrates seasonally
A microscopic bacterium found in soil
An introduced non-native species that establishes itself, spreads rapidly, and harms native biodiversity by outcompeting local organisms
A plant that cannot reproduce without human help

questions.q: How can untreated sewage entering a river cause the death of fish?
a: By making the water too salty
By increasing dissolved oxygen levels instantly
By poisoning fish with pure vitamins
By introducing organic waste that stimulates rapid bacterial growth; bacteria respire aerobically, depleting dissolved oxygen in the water and causing fish to suffocate

questions.q: What is the primary human source of sulfur dioxide emissions leading to acid rain?
a: Burning fossil fuels in power stations and heavy industry
Using chemical fertilizers on farms
Releasing aerosols containing CFCs
Disposing of household plastics

questions.q: Which of the following is a direct consequence of plastic waste accumulation in terrestrial and aquatic environments?
a: Enhanced soil aeration
Entanglement and ingestion of plastics by wildlife, leading to injury or death
Increased plant growth rates
Purification of polluted groundwater

questions.q: What is a major cause of increased atmospheric methane concentrations?
a: Volcanic eruptions under the ocean
Photosynthesis by ancient trees
Agriculture, particularly cattle farming (livestock digestion) and rice paddy fields
Exhaust fumes from electric vehicles

questions.q: What measures can be taken to reduce the impact of acid rain?
a: Adding more sulfur to coal power plants
Building taller factory chimneys without filters
Banning all rain globally
Using low-sulfur fuels, fitting flue gas desulfurization equipment (scrubbers) to power stations, and using renewable energy sources

questions.q: Why are rainforests often referred to as the 'lungs of the Earth' even though net oxygen contribution is balanced?
a: They store vast amounts of carbon and host immense biodiversity, but their destruction releases massive amounts of stored carbon dioxide
They produce all the oxygen humans breathe
They clean industrial smoke directly
They cool ocean currents

questions.q: What is the ecological impact of introducing a non-native species without natural predators into an ecosystem?
a: It helps native species grow faster
It can outcompete native species for food and habitat, leading to a decline or extinction of local wildlife
It purifies polluted rivers instantly
It stops global warming

questions.q: What is a sustainable resource?
a: A resource that is consumed entirely within one year
A resource that is mined until completely exhausted
A resource that can be produced at the same rate as it is consumed, ensuring it does not run out
A synthetic chemical created in a laboratory

questions.q: How do national parks and nature reserves contribute to conservation?
a: By allowing unrestricted industrial logging
By building large cities inside protected zones
By turning wild habitats into agricultural farmlands
By protecting habitats from human exploitation, urban development, and poaching, thereby safeguarding endangered biodiversity

questions.q: Which of the following is a consequence of agricultural land runoff containing excess nitrates and phosphates?
a: Eutrophication in nearby lakes and rivers
Improved health of aquatic plants
Decrease in algae populations
Lower water temperatures

questions.q: What is the role of recycling materials such as glass, paper, and metal?
a: To increase the volume of waste in landfills
To conserve raw materials, reduce energy consumption, and minimize environmental pollution
To create more greenhouse gases
To destroy natural ecosystems

questions.q: What is the main danger of microplastics in aquatic food webs?
a: They provide essential vitamins to fish
They dissolve completely into harmless water molecules
They can be ingested by small aquatic organisms and pass up the food chain, accumulating toxins in apex predators
They increase the population of coral reefs

questions.q: Which international action or agreement is typically aimed at reducing global greenhouse gas emissions?
a: Banning all international trade
Stopping the production of paper books
Eliminating agriculture worldwide
International climate conferences and treaties (such as the Paris Agreement) committing nations to emission reduction targets
